note.explanation: Exothermic reactions release heat to the surroundings, while endothermic reactions absorb heat. Bond breaking absorbs energy; bond formation releases energy. To find the overall enthalpy change, add the energy used to break bonds to the energy released when new bonds form.
examples: When hydrogen and oxygen form water, heat is released: ΔH = −571.6 kJ for the reaction as written.
For H₂(g) + I₂(g) → 2HI(g), the bond-energy calculation using the values in Example 5.2 gives ΔH = 436 + 151 + 2(−299) = −11 kJ.
note.checkAnswer: Bond breaking absorbs energy, so it is endothermic.
note.simple: If a reaction gives heat out, it is exothermic. If it takes heat in, it is endothermic.
note.checkQuestion: Why is breaking a chemical bond endothermic?
note.title: Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions
steps: Identify which bonds break and which bonds form.
Add the energies absorbed to break the bonds.
Add the energies released when the new bonds form, using negative values where given.
Add the two totals to find the enthalpy change, ΔH.
A negative ΔH means the reaction is exothermic; a positive ΔH means it is endothermic.
note.answer: Exothermic reactions release heat; endothermic reactions absorb heat.

options: The reaction takes heat from its surroundings.
The reaction releases heat to its surroundings.
The container must become colder.
The reaction cannot be reversed.
mcqs.stem: Which statement describes an exothermic reaction?
rationales: This describes an endothermic reaction, which absorbs heat.
This is correct: an exothermic reaction evolves heat to its surroundings.
An exothermic reaction tends to warm its surroundings and container, not cool them.
Exothermic reactions can be reversed; the reverse reaction absorbs energy.

options: ΔH is positive.
ΔH is negative.
ΔH is always zero.
The sign of ΔH cannot be known.
mcqs.stem: A reaction evolves heat. What is the sign of its enthalpy change?
rationales: A positive ΔH indicates that heat is absorbed.
This is correct: heat-evolving reactions have a negative ΔH.
ΔH is not generally zero when heat is evolved.
The information that heat is evolved is enough to determine the sign.

options: Bond breaking releases energy.
Bond formation absorbs energy.
Bond breaking absorbs energy.
Bond formation has no energy change.
mcqs.stem: Which statement about a chemical bond is correct?
rationales: Bond breaking requires energy; it does not release it.
Bond formation releases energy rather than absorbing it.
This is correct: energy must be supplied to break a bond.
Bond formation involves an energy change and releases energy.

options: The energy released by forming bonds is greater than the energy absorbed breaking bonds.
The energy absorbed breaking bonds is greater than the energy released forming bonds.
No bonds are broken in an exothermic reaction.
The products must have more energy than the reactants.
mcqs.stem: Why can a reaction that breaks and forms bonds be exothermic overall?
rationales: This is correct: greater energy release during bond formation gives a net release of energy.
This would mean more energy is absorbed than released, making the reaction endothermic.
Chemical reactions commonly involve bond breaking as well as bond formation.
For an exothermic reaction, the products have lower enthalpy than the reactants.

options: Heat is absorbed, and the container tends to cool.
Heat is evolved, and the container tends to cool.
Heat is absorbed, and the container tends to warm.
No heat is transferred.
mcqs.stem: What happens to the surroundings when a reaction absorbs heat from them?
rationales: This is correct: the reaction takes heat from its surroundings, lowering their temperature.
Heat evolution would tend to warm the surroundings, not cool them.
Absorbing heat from the surroundings does not warm them.
Heat is transferred because the reaction absorbs it from its surroundings.

options: The reverse reaction releases the same amount of heat.
The reverse reaction absorbs the same amount of heat.
The reverse reaction has no enthalpy change.
The reverse reaction is always impossible.
mcqs.stem: A forward reaction releases 80 kJ of heat. If it is reversed, what happens to the heat change?
rationales: Reversing the reaction reverses the direction of the heat change.
This is correct: the reverse reaction absorbs the amount released in the forward direction.
The reverse reaction has an enthalpy change of equal size and opposite sign.
A reaction may be reversible even though its reverse direction requires energy.

options: Energy absorbed to break bonds minus energy released forming bonds
Energy released forming bonds minus energy absorbed breaking bonds
The number of bonds broken multiplied by the temperature
The heat capacity of the reaction container
mcqs.stem: Which calculation gives ΔH when bond-formation energies are written as negative values?
rationales: This is correct: add the bond-breaking energy to the negative bond-formation energy.
This reverses the calculation when bond-formation energies are already written as negative values.
Bond count and temperature alone do not give the enthalpy change.
The container's heat capacity is not the bond-energy calculation for ΔH.

options: Combustion of a fuel
Melting ice
Evaporation of water
Decomposition of water by absorbing heat
mcqs.stem: Which process is an example of an exothermic change described in this section?
rationales: This is correct: combustion of fuels releases heat.
Melting ice absorbs heat, so it is endothermic.
Evaporation absorbs heat from the surroundings.
A decomposition that absorbs heat is endothermic.

written.text: Hydrogen gas and oxygen gas react to give liquid water in an exothermic reaction.

rubric.why: The balanced chemical equation identifies the reaction and its products.
rubric.description: Write the balanced equation for forming water.
rubric.how: Show two moles of hydrogen reacting with one mole of oxygen to form two moles of water.

rubric.why: The heat amount and its direction show the exothermic nature of the reaction.
rubric.description: State the heat evolved and the enthalpy change.
rubric.how: Show that 571.6 kJ is released and that ΔH is negative.

modelAnswer: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l) + 571.6 kJ
571.6 kJ heat energy is evolved during this reaction.
If the energy evolved is shown separately it is expressed as ΔH = −571.6 kJ.

written.text:
Calculate the enthalpy change of the following chemical reaction.

H₂(g) + I₂(g) → 2 HI(g)

Bond energies of H₂, I₂ and HI are 436,151, and -299 kJ mol⁻¹ respectively.

rubric.why: The H₂ and I₂ bonds must be broken, which absorbs energy.
rubric.description: Add the energies for breaking the reactant bonds.
rubric.how: Use 436 kJ mol⁻¹ for H₂ and 151 kJ mol⁻¹ for I₂.

rubric.why: Two HI bonds form, and the given formation energy is negative.
rubric.description: Include the energy released in forming two HI bonds.
rubric.how: Multiply −299 kJ mol⁻¹ by 2.

rubric.why: Combining bond breaking and bond formation gives the overall enthalpy change.
rubric.description: Add the bond-energy contributions.
rubric.how: Evaluate the sum using the signed bond-formation energy.

rubric.why: The final signed result gives the reaction's enthalpy change.
rubric.description: State the final enthalpy change.
rubric.how: Give the calculated result in kJ.

modelAnswer: Energy absorbed to break H₂ and I₂ bonds = 436 + 151 = 587 kJ.
Energy evolved in forming two HI bonds = 2(−299) = −598 kJ.
The enthalpy change is ΔH = −11 kJ.

written.text: Why is breaking of a bond an endothermic process?
written.finalAnswer: Energy must be absorbed to overcome the forces holding the bonded atoms together.

rubric.why: Identifying energy absorption establishes that bond breaking is endothermic.
rubric.description: State what happens to energy when a bond breaks.
rubric.how: Say that energy is absorbed or supplied.

rubric.why: The explanation connects the energy input to separating atoms that are bonded.
rubric.description: Explain why energy is needed.
rubric.how: Explain that energy overcomes the attraction holding the bonded atoms together.

modelAnswer: Energy is absorbed to overcome the forces holding the bonded atoms together.
Therefore, breaking a bond is an endothermic process.

written.text: Explain why formation of a bond is always an exothermic process.
written.finalAnswer: When a bond forms, the atoms reach a lower-energy, more stable state and energy is released.

rubric.why: The answer must identify the process being explained.
rubric.description: State what happens when a bond forms.
rubric.how: Explain that atoms become bonded.

rubric.why: Energy release is the defining feature that makes the process exothermic.
rubric.description: State the energy change.
rubric.how: Say that energy is released or evolved during bond formation.

rubric.why: The lower-energy state explains why energy is given out.
rubric.description: Relate bond formation to the energy state of the atoms.
rubric.how: State that the bonded atoms are in a lower-energy or more stable state.

rubric.why: The final classification answers the question directly.
rubric.description: Name the process.
rubric.how: Conclude that bond formation is exothermic.

modelAnswer: When atoms form a bond, they move to a lower-energy, more stable state.
The energy difference is released to the surroundings.
Therefore, formation of a bond is an exothermic process.

written.text:
Find out the enthalpy change of the following reaction using the given data.

N₂ + O₂ → 2NO

Bond dissociation energy of N₂ = 958.38 kJ/mol
Bond dissociation energy of O₂ = 498 kJ/mol
Bond formation energy of NO = −626 kJ/mol

rubric.why: Breaking the N₂ and O₂ bonds absorbs energy.
rubric.description: Calculate the energy absorbed for bond breaking.
rubric.how: Add the two bond dissociation energies.

rubric.why: Two NO bonds form for the reaction as written, so the formation energy is counted twice.
rubric.description: Calculate the energy released in NO bond formation.
rubric.how: Multiply −626 kJ mol⁻¹ by 2.

rubric.why: The bond-breaking total is needed to obtain the overall enthalpy change.
rubric.description: Show the total energy absorbed.
rubric.how: Evaluate 958.38 + 498.

rubric.why: The released energy must be combined with the absorbed energy using its sign.
rubric.description: Combine the breaking and formation contributions.
rubric.how: Add 1456.38 kJ and −1252 kJ.

rubric.why: The positive final value identifies the endothermic enthalpy change.
rubric.description: State the final enthalpy change.
rubric.how: Give the signed answer in kJ.

modelAnswer: Energy absorbed to break N₂ and O₂ bonds = 958.38 + 498 = 1456.38 kJ.
Energy evolved in forming two NO bonds = 2(−626) = −1252 kJ.
The positive enthalpy change shows that the reaction is endothermic.

written.text: Explain why the reaction between atmospheric gases oxygen and nitrogen does not take place under normal conditions? But in the presence of lightning these gases react to give NO. The reaction stops as soon as the lightning stops.
written.finalAnswer: The reaction is highly endothermic and needs the energy supplied by lightning; without that energy, it does not proceed under normal conditions.

rubric.why: Naming the reactants and product identifies the reaction being discussed.
rubric.description: Identify the reaction.
rubric.how: State that atmospheric nitrogen and oxygen react to form NO.

rubric.why: Its energy requirement explains why it does not occur readily in ordinary conditions.
rubric.description: Describe the energy nature of the reaction.
rubric.how: State that the reaction is highly endothermic or absorbs a large amount of energy.

rubric.why: Lightning supplies the energy needed for the reaction to occur.
rubric.description: Explain the role of lightning.
rubric.how: Say that lightning provides enough energy for the reaction.

rubric.why: This explains why the reaction stops when the energy supply ends.
rubric.description: Explain why the reaction stops when lightning stops.
rubric.how: State that the reaction needs continuing energy input.

modelAnswer: The reaction between atmospheric nitrogen and oxygen to form NO is highly endothermic.
It does not occur under normal conditions because it needs a large input of energy.
Lightning supplies enough energy for the reaction to take place.
When the lightning stops, the energy supply stops and so does the reaction.

written.text: A reaction between natural gas (CH₄) and atmospheric oxygen does not take place when you mix them. As soon as you show a burning match stick, the reaction starts immediately and then it continues until one or both of the reactants is/are used up. Explain.
written.finalAnswer: The burning match supplies the initial energy needed to start combustion. Once started, the exothermic reaction releases heat that keeps it going until a reactant is used up.

rubric.why: Identifying the reactants sets out the combustion reaction.
rubric.description: Identify the substances reacting.
rubric.how: Name methane or natural gas and atmospheric oxygen.

rubric.why: The match provides the energy that starts the reaction.
rubric.description: Explain why the match is needed initially.
rubric.how: State that the burning match supplies energy to start combustion.

rubric.why: Heat released by the reaction explains how it continues after ignition.
rubric.description: Explain why the reaction continues.
rubric.how: State that combustion is exothermic and releases heat.

rubric.why: Combustion stops when a required reactant is no longer available.
rubric.description: State when the reaction ends.
rubric.how: Say that it continues until one or both reactants are used up.

modelAnswer: Mixing methane and oxygen does not provide enough initial energy to start the reaction.
A burning match supplies the energy needed to start combustion.
Combustion is exothermic, so the heat released helps the reaction continue.
The reaction continues until one or both reactants are used up.

written.text: Explain the difference between the terms heat and enthalpy.
written.finalAnswer: Heat is energy transferred during a reaction; enthalpy is the energy content of a system, and enthalpy change is the heat evolved or absorbed during a reaction at constant pressure.

rubric.why: The answer must describe heat as energy transferred or exchanged.
rubric.description: Define heat in the context of a reaction.
rubric.how: State that heat is evolved or absorbed during a reaction.

rubric.why: Enthalpy refers to the energy content of the system, not simply energy being transferred.
rubric.description: Define enthalpy.
rubric.how: Identify enthalpy as the energy content of a system.

rubric.why: Distinguishing enthalpy from its change clarifies the terms.
rubric.description: Explain what enthalpy change represents.
rubric.how: Say that ΔH represents the heat evolved or absorbed during the reaction.

rubric.why: The constant-pressure condition connects the heat transfer with enthalpy change.
rubric.description: State the condition for the heat–enthalpy-change relation.
rubric.how: Mention that at constant pressure, the heat exchanged equals ΔH.

modelAnswer: Heat is energy transferred to or from a system during a change.
Enthalpy is the energy content of a system.
The enthalpy change, ΔH, is the heat evolved or absorbed during a reaction at constant pressure.
Thus, heat is energy transfer, while enthalpy describes the system's energy content.

written.text: Explain the role of lipids in our body.
written.finalAnswer: Lipids are biological fuels; during metabolism, their chemical energy is converted into heat that helps keep the body warm.

rubric.description: Name the process that releases the energy.
rubric.how: Mention metabolism.

rubric.why: This connects the fuel to the energy change in the body.
rubric.description: Describe what happens to the fuel's energy.

rubric.why: The heat produced explains how this process helps the body.

During metabolism, the chemical energy in food is converted into heat energy.

written.text: Why is it essential to cook some of the food items while others we can eat without cooking?
written.finalAnswer: Cooking supplies energy that can bring about changes in some foods; foods that do not need those changes can be eaten without cooking.

rubric.why: The response should link the difference to whether heating or a change is needed.
rubric.description: Connect the two cases.
rubric.how: Explain that the need for cooking depends on the changes and energy required.

modelAnswer: Cooking supplies heat energy and brings about changes in food.
Some foods need these changes before they are eaten.
Other foods can be eaten without cooking because they do not need those changes first.

written.text: Why does fireworks look spectacular? What type of chemical compounds undergo chemical reactions during this activity?
written.finalAnswer: Fireworks produce heat, light and sound during combustion; different metal salts, along with oxidising agents, undergo the reactions and produce different colours.

rubric.why: Heat, light and sound account for the spectacular effects.
rubric.description: Name the effects produced by fireworks.
rubric.how: State that fireworks yield heat, light and sound.

rubric.why: Combustion is the chemical process described for fireworks.
rubric.description: Identify the type of reaction.
rubric.how: Name combustion reactions.

modelAnswer: Fireworks are the result of combustion reactions that yield heat, light and sound.
Different metal salts produce a variety of colours when burnt.

examTips: A short-answer question may ask you to define exothermic or endothermic reactions. Include whether heat is evolved or absorbed.

For an explanation question about bonds, state both processes: bond breaking absorbs energy, while bond formation releases energy.
When asked about the reverse reaction, state that the same amount of energy is exchanged in the opposite direction.

example.question: Hydrogen gas and oxygen gas react to give liquid water in an exothermic reaction.

explain.title: Heat of a reaction
explain.body: Heat, which is evolved or absorbed during a chemical reaction, is called the heat of that reaction.

explain.title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions
explain.body: Chemical reactions in which heat energy is evolved are called exothermic reactions while those in which heat energy is absorbed are called endothermic reactions. Heat from an exothermic reaction goes to the surroundings and container, making them warmer. An endothermic reaction takes heat from the surroundings, so the container becomes cooler.

explain.title: The sign of ΔH
explain.body: When energy evolved is shown separately, an exothermic reaction has a negative ΔH. An endothermic reaction has a positive ΔH. Reversing a reaction reverses the direction of the heat change.

explain.title: Bond energy and the overall reaction
explain.body: Breaking bonds absorbs energy, while forming bonds evolves energy. The overall reaction is exothermic if more energy is released by bond formation than is absorbed in bond breaking. It is endothermic if more energy is absorbed than released.

explain.title: Exothermic reactions in everyday life
explain.body: Combustion of fuels releases heat used for cooking, heating and generating electricity. During metabolism, chemical energy in food is converted to heat. Fireworks are combustion reactions that produce heat, light and sound.

mistakes: Do not give a positive ΔH for a reaction that evolves heat; its ΔH is negative.
Do not say that bond breaking releases energy. Breaking a bond absorbs energy.
Do not forget to multiply a bond energy by the number of bonds formed or broken.
When bond-formation energy is given as a negative value, keep its negative sign in the calculation.
Do not assume that the reverse reaction has the same sign of ΔH; it has the opposite sign.
In a bond-energy calculation, show both the bond-breaking and bond-forming contributions before giving the final answer.
